claims.text: Rapid melt spinning of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 occurs at cooling rates greater than 10^5 K/s.
Rapidly melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 typically contains several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
An immediate microsecond-scale reheating pulse after melt spinning will increase amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The pulse reheating will increase the alloy's thermal stability.
Pulse reheating can bypass the critical temperature window for nucleation.
The pulse should raise the sample to just below the crystallization onset, described as near the glass-transition temperature.
A microsecond-scale thermal pulse leaves insufficient time for atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
Suppressing atomic diffusion and rearrangement blocks nucleation and growth of the primary crystalline phases.
Rapid traversal of the crystallization-temperature window freezes in a metastable amorphous structure.
Retention of the metastable amorphous structure will simplify the crystallization-event signature during subsequent reheating.
Pulse-treated samples will have a higher amorphous fraction than samples processed without the pulse.
Pulse-treated samples will show a singular, elevated glass-transition region by DSC.
Pulse-treated samples will show a delayed or diminished crystallization exotherm relative to untreated samples.
Standard rapid melt-spinning processing of this alloy produces extensive primary crystallization and a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
The relevant post-treatment assessment boundary is DSC reheating at 5–10 K/min.
Exceeding the intended nucleation or crystallization threshold during pulse reheating may cause inadvertent crystallization.

contradictions.description: The intervention and boundary require the pulse to remain just below crystallization onset, whereas the mechanism says that reheating rapidly passes through the critical crystallization-temperature window. It is therefore unclear whether the proposed trajectory avoids that window or traverses it.

The pulse is said to preserve a metastable amorphous state after melt spinning, but the stated initial and baseline condition already includes extensive primary crystallization. No mechanism is given by which a sub-onset pulse would remove crystals that formed during solidification.
